title: On-call runway and incident journey timelines with contextual alert cards
creator: Maya Patel
description: Goal: Design an "on-call runway" view that helps on-call engineers understand an active incident's trajectory, key alert context, SLO impact, and immediate next actions without jumping between multiple console pages. Scope includes: 1) an incident timeline with zoom/scrub controls showing alert spikes, rollout events, and KV-cache/cache-hit annotations; 2) contextual alert cards in the right rail that surface runbooks, recent related commits/PRs, and suggested mitigations; 3) a compact postmortem quick-link module that collects relevant traces, SLO deltas, and error-rate charts for handoff and retrospective. Success metrics: reduce average investigation time by 15% for common alert classes (latency/backpressure), reduce cross-page navigation (console route switches) by 40% in incident workflows, and achieve SUS >= 80 in follow-up usability tests.
acceptance_criteria: A fully functional high-fidelity prototype (Figma) that demonstrates timeline zoom and scrub and shows alert-card interactions
Right-rail alert cards present: alert summary, top 3 correlated signals, link to runbook, link to last deploy/PR, and 'mark as investigated' action
Postmortem quick-link module aggregates: timeline snapshot, SLO delta table, and 'create postmortem' CTA that carries context to PM's template
Usability session (n=6) with on-call engineers yields no major usability blockers and identifies at most 3 actionable tweaks
Design handoff assets and acceptance notes uploaded to Confluence and a design review scheduled with Eng and PM
comments: 2026-03-09 Maya Patel: Kickoff — sketched initial flows: timeline as primary canvas, alert cards docked to the right, postmortem quick-link as ephemeral drawer. PM aligned on success metrics. Asked Eng to provide list of signal types (latency, error-rate, kv-cache-miss) we can surface.
2026-03-11 Ethan Ruiz: Initial wireframes posted to Figma. Requested tighter spacing on cards and a visual affordance for 'silence' vs 'acknowledge'. Asked SRE to validate suggested mitigations list.

2026-03-12 Feedback session with SRE (Anika Shah): prefer a 'runbook score' and explicit deploy delta link. Engineering flagged potential backend work for aggregating correlated signals (see ENG-6044).

2026-03-13 Design critique: PM (Liam O'Connor) requested an explicit CTA to create a postmortem from the timeline. Decided to add a time-range selector that feeds the postmortem snapshot. Action: update prototype and schedule 1:1 with product writer for copy.

2026-03-14 Ethan Ruiz: High-fidelity prototype updated; added timeline scrubber, card hover state, and 'create postmortem' modal mock. Scheduled usability sessions for 2026-03-16 and linked test script in Confluence.
decisions: Use a single-page incident runway rather than cross-page widgets to reduce context switching
Alert cards will include three signal types by default (latency, error-rate, resource-saturation) with an expandable list
Postmortem creation will carry a time-range payload derived from the timeline scrubber to pre-populate SLO deltas and top traces
Primary action for alerts is 'acknowledge' with secondary 'silence' and tertiary 'create postmortem'
next_steps: Finalize Figma prototype and export interaction specification (Ethan) — due 2026-03-18
Run two moderated usability tests with on-call engineers (Maya) — sessions on 2026-03-16 and 2026-03-17
Work with ENG to scope telemetry endpoints for correlated signals (ENG-6044) and timeline events (ENG-5912)
Prepare design handoff package and schedule cross-team review (Design, Eng, PM, SRE) — target 2026-03-20
notes: Trade-offs: adding more correlated signals increases backend cost and latency for the incident page; we will prioritize three and allow custom expansion
Alternate considered: inline postmortem composer vs navigation to PM template; chose composer for context carryover but will keep link to full PM template
Edge cases: multi-incident merge — timeline will show layers with opacity and a selector to focus on a single incident
